snippet.title: Perfectly Straight Fencelines With A Drone Explained!
snippet.description:
Get dead-straight fence lines without guessing or rework.
This simple drone trick can save time, labour, and costly mistakes.

In this video, I’m with Jake Booker in steep country near Tumut NSW, showing how a basic drone can be used like a scope to line up fence posts with surprising accuracy. By using built-in grid settings, you can project a straight line over long distances and set posts within around 50mm accuracy — even across steep hills.

This matters because poor alignment wastes time and effort, as well as weakening your fence and causing misalignment with existing fences. Whether you’re fencing new ground or replacing old lines, this method gives you a repeatable, visual system that improves accuracy and efficiency on the job.

If you’re a fencing contractor, farmer, or property owner working in uneven country, this is a practical tool worth understanding.

This video covers drone fence line setup, how to use DJI grid and crosshair overlays for alignment, fencing accuracy techniques, and practical applications for rural property fencing. It’s relevant for Australian, US, and UK farmers looking to improve fencing efficiency, reduce errors, and adopt simple technology in the field.

snippet.title: Biodiversity Farming: Trees That Boost Profit
snippet.description:
Trees don’t have to cost you production — they can actually improve it.
This farm proves biodiversity, carbon, and profit can work together.

I’m at Yan Yan Gurt West in Victoria with Andrew and Hugh Stewart, where 30 years of tree planting has transformed a traditional livestock farm into a highly resilient, biodiverse system — without reducing output.

We break down how increasing woody vegetation from 3% to 19% of farm area has:

Maintained prime lamb and wool production
Improved drought resilience and shelter
Reduced erosion and salinity
Created new income streams through timber, seed, and biodiversity
Offset livestock emissions through carbon sequestration

You’ll also learn practical, in-paddock techniques for:

Where to plant trees (and why dead trees matter)
How to establish paddock trees successfully
Choosing species for climate resilience
Using biodiversity to stabilise and improve production systems

This is real-world agroforestry — not theory — built over decades.

If you’re running livestock, managing land, or thinking about tree planting, this is one of the most practical breakdowns you’ll see.

snippet.title: See what life is like in Singapore's only women's prison | Inside The Women's Prison (1/3)
snippet.description:
How do inmates survive within the strict confines of Singapore’s only women’s prison? In the first episode of this three-part series, we follow six inmates as they navigate the rigours and realities of life behind bars. 

With rising tensions and few outlets for relief, Joanna reaches her breaking point, putting her freedom at risk. After 14 years behind bars, long-buried doubts resurface when Christeen finally receives a long-awaited visit from her distant son. Yu Xin clings to simple pleasures and finds respite from monotony. Halen embraces her newfound responsibility as an IC but fears the repercussions that could land her in lockup. Juliana is forced to confront the weight of her past when she comes face-to-face with her imprisoned daughter, while Haziqah struggles with helplessness after receiving devastating news about her son.

-------

▷ 02:05 - Nur Joanna, 22, talks about how art helps her express herself
▷ 06:37 - Christeen, 47, talks about yard time and being a peer supporter

Women make up about 10% of Singapore’s prison population. And inside the walls of Institution A4, at the Changi Prison Complex, are about 800 female inmates, incarcerated for various offences.

snippet.title: A Short History of Progress and Why It’s Failing Us | Surviving Progress (Full Documentary)
snippet.description:
Inspired by Ronald Wright’s bestseller A Short History of Progress, this film is a powerful cinematic exploration of the hidden dangers behind “progress.”

Throughout human history, what we’ve called progress has often led to unintended consequences -collapsing civilizations and creating new crises. Today, those same patterns are playing out on a global scale.

Featuring insights from leading thinkers, activists, economists, and scientists, the film examines “progress traps”- innovations that solve short-term problems but create long-term risks. As these traps become embedded in our technology, economy, and way of life, the question becomes urgent:

Can humanity change course before history repeats itself?
-------

Chapters
▷ 00:01:28 - Evolution and the roots of human nature

snippet.title: Off Grid Living: How to Convince Your Partner to Leave the City for a Cabin in the Wilderness
snippet.description:
You can price out land, map out schools, and build a flawless plan and still watch your partner shut down the second you say, “Let’s move rural.” I’m recording from the cabin after a loud, rainy night, answering the question I get constantly: how do you convince your spouse or partner to embrace a more rural, hands-on, self-reliant life?

I start with the deeper why. For me, the pull toward the woods is about biology and mental health as much as preference: the quiet, the work, the sensory reality of nature, and the relief of stepping out of a hyper-digital world. But then we get practical and honest about why a partner hesitates. Kids, income, health care, aging parents, distance from friends, and the fear of losing identity are not “excuses.” They are legitimate stakes, and treating them like obstacles can damage your relationship fast.

The shift that actually helps is simple but hard: stop selling and start sharing. Lead with what you feel is missing and why it matters to who you are, then listen long enough to find the real fear under the objection. From there, I walk through what changed everything in my own marriage: experiences instead of arguments, small steps instead of a sudden leap, and compromises that turn “my dream” into “our direction.” If you want a rural lifestyle that lasts, it has to be chosen, not won.

If this hits home, subscribe, share it with someone who’s wrestling with the same conversation, and leave a review so more people can find it. What’s the biggest concern you and your partner can’t get past right now?

snippet.title: Biological Farming: Why Farmers Hold Back
snippet.description:
Biological farming is not a recipe — it is a way of thinking about soil, inputs and farm resilience.

snippet.title: Peeling and Stacking Logs for my Next Cabin
snippet.description:
Building a log cabin by hand in the woods.

Watch the process of stacking logs and preparing the site for this wilderness build. This footage captures the manual labor and techniques required to construct a structure from raw timber.
There's a particular quiet here in the morning.
Before the chainsaw. Before the work.Just the fire, a coffee, Cali at my side.
I've been filming in that quiet for years.The slow stuff. The in-between stuff.More Cali, more nature, more simple cabin life.
It never fit YouTube.Too quiet. No project reveal. Nothing to put in a thumbnail.So most of it stayed on a hard drive. Or I posted it but nobody saw it because it didn’t please the algorithm 
I kept filming it anyway, because that's the part I love most.
So I built a place.
It's called the Hearthside.
A small membership community on the My Self Reliance website.
Every month — a note from the cabin, members-only videos, a podcast episode recorded by the woodstove.Cali's at my side, as always.And a few times a year, something small in the mail from the cabin, something that evokes the feeling I get when I’m here.
$15 a month. Limited membership, so I can stay available to the people who are in it.
If you've been watching for a while and you want to go a little deeper —not just watch this life, but be part of it —that's what it's there for.

snippet.title: The Buzz About Bees in Alaska + Our Biggest Honey Harvest Yet
snippet.description:
Bees in Alaska? 

Keeping Honeybees in a notoriously cold climate may sound foreign but folks all over the state have been raising bees successfully for decades. Honeybees are primarily shipped to the 49th state in the early spring months when there is still snow on the ground. Growing the colony, watching for swarms and harvesting honey is only a portion of caring for your bees. The ultimate goal for many small-scale beekeepers in Alaska is to keep their bees over the harshest winter months, a feat not easily achieved. Strong colonies undoubtedly can repopulate much more quickly than hives that are shipped and installed year after year. 

We take a tour of Mike, Dawn & Jimmy's hives kept at the Harlow Family Farm, Georgeson Botanical Garden and the Fairbanks Community Garden.

In addition we harvest our honey from the girls and start the Fumidil- B treatment, feeding and winter preparation process.

snippet.title: Summer Has Arrived – Early Garden Harvest, Spruce Tips & Tasting Smoked Beaver
snippet.description:
After a cool spring we are more than ready for the summer heat! A quick bee update and garden harvest then we're off to pick spruce tips for a few summer concoctions - spinach pesto, oxymel, wild soda and oil infused spruce tip marinade. Duck soup is on the menu for the first night, then we try the freshly smoked beaver with cooked radishes and sourdough focaccia, all enjoyed under Alaska's midnight sun.
